messages.text:
We propose replacing the blanket approval requirement with the following terms for the three-depot trial.

1. Both project teams may use trial measurements internally to operate and evaluate the trial. Access to raw failure traces and firmware parameters is limited to named trial-team members who need them for their work. They may not forward those materials to anyone else, except under the urgent safety provision below.

2. Either party proposing an external report will send the draft to the other at least 10 working days before release. During that period, the reviewer may identify specific passages that reveal restricted material or identify a route or depot. The author may release the report once it removes those passages or both parties agree on wording. If the reviewer raises no such objection within 10 working days, the author may release the draft without further approval. The sensor maker may use this process to publish aggregate uptime pooled across all three depots, with route and depot identifiers omitted and no breakdown that would reasonably reveal either.

3. If waiting for review would delay action needed to address an urgent safety risk, either party may immediately disclose the minimum information needed to someone able to act on it. The disclosing party will notify the other as soon as practicable afterward, specifying what it shared, with whom, and why.

Does your external maintenance contractor need raw traces to perform a specific diagnostic task, or would a fault code, timestamp, and diagnostic summary let them complete the repair? We propose starting with the summary. If that leaves a specific task unresolved, our engineers can examine the trace and return the findings. If direct inspection is essential, we would consider jointly naming a specific technician to the trial team, bound by the same confidentiality terms, with access limited to the relevant trace for that task.

We can start repairs with a fault code and diagnostic summary. We can also accept the 10-working-day publication process if we agree on four points.

1. **Maintenance.** The operator may send its confidentiality-bound maintenance contractor the device identifier, fault code, and diagnostic summary needed for a repair. Use a time window unless the technician needs the precise timestamp. If the summary is insufficient, the maker’s engineers will examine the trace and return findings the technician can act on. To avoid holding up a repair, let’s jointly name a lead and backup technician before the trial. If the engineers’ findings leave a specific task unresolved and direct inspection is essential, either named technician may inspect the relevant trace under the trial team’s confidentiality terms. The operator will log the task and the access. This standing permission covers only the trace material needed for that repair.

2. **Monthly board reporting.** Before the trial, the teams will approve a standing template for the transit board showing monthly uptime and failure counts pooled across all three depots. The operator may send the completed template to the board each month without a new review. It will omit raw traces, firmware parameters, route and depot identifiers, and exact event times. It will combine or suppress entries where a small count or other detail could reasonably identify an employee, route, or depot. The template may be used in public board papers on the same terms.

3. **Serious incidents and urgent risks.** The operator’s safety lead may promptly notify the relevant authorities of a serious incident and provide necessary follow-up information without prior notice or clearance, including when the immediate hazard has passed. We also accept your proposed urgent-risk exception for either party. In both cases, the disclosing party will share the information required or reasonably needed and tell the other party what it shared, with whom, and why as soon as practicable and legally permitted.

4. **Other publications.** For reports outside the board template, including the maker’s pooled uptime report, each party will designate a publication contact. The author will send the draft to the other contact at least 10 working days before release. An objection must identify the passage and explain how it reveals restricted technical material or could reasonably identify an employee, route, or depot, including through a combination of place and time. The author’s contact may authorize release after the review period if no such objection arrives. If one does, the author may release the report after removing the objected-to material, or both contacts may approve revised wording.

We accept all four clauses as written. Together they replace the draft’s blanket confidentiality and prior-approval requirement for trial measurements. Both project teams may use the measurements internally to operate and evaluate the trial.

The jointly named lead and backup technicians are trial-team members for the limited purpose of the trace inspection described in clause 1. Routine repairs use the diagnostic summary. Firmware parameters remain restricted to named trial-team members who need them, subject to the disclosures permitted by clause 3.

Before the trial, we will work with you to name the technicians, approve the monthly board template, and exchange publication contacts. Under clause 4, we may publish uptime pooled across all three depots after the 10-working-day review period if no qualifying objection arrives.

We propose two sign-off amendments so a safety review and a time-sensitive repair can proceed on separate clocks.

**Board reporting.** The monthly board paper will retain the agreed three-depot totals and suppression rules. Before release, the operator’s reporting lead will also check whether a reader could reconstruct a suppressed result by subtracting published figures, including figures in earlier reports. We propose keeping depot breakdowns out of the standing public template.

For confidential oversight, we propose a trigger of **one serious safety incident or two safety-related failures of the same type within a rolling 30-day period**. Before the trial, both teams will record the qualifying incident and failure categories in the reporting protocol. When the safety lead verifies and logs a trigger, they may give designated members of the confidential board subcommittee access to the relevant suppressed results within one working day, without waiting for the monthly paper or maker clearance. Members will receive only the detail needed to assess the event, through a restricted board channel. Exact depot and time may be shown together only if the safety lead records why both are necessary. Those details stay out of public minutes.

**Contractor access.** For a device held out of service after an incident, we propose a 30-minute access target. The clock starts when the operator’s maintenance duty lead records that the diagnostic summary leaves a specific return-to-service question unresolved and identifies the part of the incident trace needed to answer it. The duty lead may then give the jointly named lead or backup technician read-only access to that portion within 30 minutes. The maker’s engineers can assist in parallel. The duty lead will notify the maker when access opens, log who viewed the trace, and close access when the task ends. The existing summary-first process continues for routine repairs.

Neither trigger delays the safety lead’s notice to authorities. The agreed publication contacts and 10-working-day review period continue to govern other publications. Can your team support the 30-minute target through standing access for the two named technicians, and do you agree to the proposed subcommittee trigger?

Yes. We support standing authorization for the two named technicians to meet the 30-minute target, and we accept the proposed subcommittee trigger. We propose the following addendum.

1. **Public reporting.** The standing monthly board paper may show uptime and failure counts pooled across all three depots, with no depot breakdowns. At a single-vehicle depot, even an uptime figure can identify the vehicle’s operator. Before release, the reporting lead will check whether a reader could identify an employee, route, or depot, or reconstruct a suppressed result by combining current and earlier figures. If so, the lead will combine reporting periods or suppress enough figures to prevent that inference. We will apply the same check to our pooled uptime publications under the agreed 10-working-day review process.

2. **Confidential board oversight.** The trigger is one serious safety incident or two safety-related failures of the same type within a rolling 30-day period. Both teams will record the qualifying categories before the trial. Within one working day after verifying and logging a trigger, the safety lead may give designated subcommittee members the relevant suppressed results and a diagnostic summary through the restricted board channel, without maker clearance. The summary may describe what failed, the safety consequence, and the corrective action. Exact depot and time may appear together only where the lead records why both are necessary. Raw traces and firmware parameters stay within the trial team. Public minutes follow the public reporting rules.

3. **Time-sensitive repair.** For a device held out of service after an incident, the 30-minute access target starts when the maintenance duty lead logs the return-to-service question left unresolved by the summary and identifies the trace portion essential to answer it. The lead may then open read-only access for either named technician under the trial team’s confidentiality terms. The repair view will exclude firmware parameters. The lead will notify us when access opens, log who viewed the trace, and close access when the task ends. Our engineers may assist in parallel. Routine repairs follow the agreed summary-first process.

The existing serious-incident and urgent-risk exceptions apply across all three tiers. Notice to authorities may proceed immediately, independently of either clock.
